Depth as Time in One-Step Generative Models

Arnold Caleb Asiimwe    William Yang    Sanghyuk Chun    Esin Tureci    Olga Russakovsky
Princeton University
Abstract

The recent wave of one-step generative models, which compress the multi-step trajectory of diffusion via either distillation or learned flow maps, has reached an inflection point where they can generate high-quality images. Here, we ask a natural question that follows from these advances: what happens to the denoising trajectory of multi-step diffusion when generation is compressed into a single forward pass? We offer an empirical observation we call depth as time: the denoising computation that multi-step diffusion performs across sampling steps appears to unfold across the depth of a single forward pass, and can be recovered by decoding intermediate layers with the model’s own output head. Most interestingly, we show that this depthwise computation depends on the transport task a flow map is trained to solve. The most surprising case is MeanFlow, where probing shorter transport intervals reveals both denoising and renoising within a single network evaluation. In contrast, generators trained without a time-indexed transport task, such as drifting models, do not exhibit the same depthwise denoising. Consequently, we show that models that exhibit the depthwise denoising phenomenon are more compressible across the layerwise computation: a MeanFlow SiT-L/2 model can be compressed by 16.6×16.6\times in parameters into a single time-conditioned block. Together, these results suggest that the temporal computation of diffusion is not eliminated by one-step generation, but reorganized across network depth. Code is available.

1 Introduction

One-step generative models based on diffusion have recently been shown to produce high-quality images without the iterative denoising trajectory of multi-step diffusion, using methods ranging from distillation (Salimans and Ho, 2022, Luo et al., 2023, Yin et al., 2024, Zhou et al., 2024) to directly learning flow maps (Song et al., 2023, Frans et al., 2025, Boffi et al., 2025, Geng et al., 2025). This efficiency, however, seems to remove a defining feature of diffusion- and flow-based generation: the explicit trajectory of intermediate states that evolves from coarse to fine-grained detail. This trajectory provides a natural axis for intervention and control via guidance methods that modify the generative vector field depending on the desired goal. Several downstream advantages of multi-step diffusion have followed, ranging from classifier-free guidance (Ho and Salimans, 2022, Wang et al., 2026), reinforcement-learning-based control (Black et al., 2024, Wallace et al., 2024, Fan et al., 2023), and image editing (Meng et al., 2021, Lee et al., 2026, Liang et al., 2026) to classification (Li et al., 2023, Clark and Jaini, 2023), fine-grained generation (Guo et al., 2026, Zarei et al., 2026), and many others.

It is natural, therefore, to ask what happens to this denoising trajectory when generation is compressed into a single forward pass. We show that distilled one-step models and flow maps effectively unroll this loop across network depth, and that decoding their intermediate blocks reveals a coarse-to-fine progression reminiscent of the one multi-step diffusion exposes across sampling steps. We call this observation depth as time. In contrast, one-step models not based on diffusion, such as drifting models (Deng et al., 2026), do not appear to exhibit the same transport-organized depthwise trajectory.

Surprisingly, depth as time can be observed without any additional training. Applying the model’s own output head to its intermediate representations recovers a layerwise velocity (Sec. 3.1), from which we decode the image at each depth and reveal a progressive, denoising-like pattern (Sec. 3.2).

Importantly, the depthwise trajectory depends on the transport task the model is asked to solve at inference. This becomes especially clear when the model generates a noisy intermediate 𝐱r\mathbf{x}_{r} rather than the clean endpoint 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0}. Distilled one-step models under multi-step sampling nest depth as time within sampling time, with each sampler step carrying its own depthwise refinement (Sec. 4.1). Flow maps conditioned on the transport endpoint such as MeanFlow (Geng et al., 2025) and Shortcut models (Frans et al., 2025) instead exhibit a non-monotonic denoise-then-renoise pattern, first revealing cleaner image structure before renoising toward the requested noisy endpoint (Sec. 4.2).

Finally, in Sec. 5, we treat depth as time explicitly by training a single time-conditioned block to denoise across layers, yielding an even more compressed one-step generator. For example, we compress a MeanFlow SiT-L/2 one-step model for ImageNet-256×256256\times 256 generation by 16.6×16.6\times (from 459459M to 27.627.6M parameters) at FID 11.711.7, which improves to 4.94.9 with FD-loss post-training (Yang et al., 2026), compared with 4.04.0 for the original model. Performing the same compression on a drifting model, by contrast, degrades it to a FID of 47.147.1.

2 Preliminaries: One-step Generative Models

Diffusion- or flow-based generative models transport a simple noise distribution toward the data distribution along a time-indexed stochastic or deterministic process (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015, Song et al., 2021, Liu et al., 2022, Lipman et al., 2022, Albergo et al., 2023). In the ordinary differential equation (ODE) formulation, the learned vector field specifies the instantaneous velocity with which samples evolve along this transport, and sampling amounts to numerically integrating it, conventionally requiring repeated network evaluations. A long-standing goal has therefore been to approximate this transport using only a few network evaluations—or even a single one—while preserving sample quality. Existing approaches broadly include distillation-based methods, which transfer the behavior of a multi-step teacher to a faster student through flow-map or distribution-level objectives (Salimans and Ho, 2022, Luo et al., 2023, Yin et al., 2024, Zhou et al., 2024, Sauer et al., 2024a, Sauer et al., 2024b), and methods that learn few-step models (or flow maps) from scratch (Song et al., 2023, Frans et al., 2025, Boffi et al., 2025, Geng et al., 2025, Zhou et al., 2025).

Flow maps (Boffi et al., 2025), in particular, provide a useful description of recent one-step generative models based on diffusion. A flow map Φt→r\Phi_{t\rightarrow r} denotes the transport induced by integrating the ODE from time tt to time rr. Throughout, we use transport task to refer to the specific map Φt→r\Phi_{t\rightarrow r} that a network is trained to approximate, i.e., the samplewise correspondence between noise level tt and endpoint rr that its output must realize; this is distinct from the downstream task (e.g., class-conditional generation) that the model serves. Learned flow maps can be classified by their transport task: approximating Φt→0​(𝐱t)\Phi_{t\rightarrow 0}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) for Song et al. (2023) and Geng et al. (2024), Φt→r​(𝐱t)\Phi_{t\rightarrow r}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) for Kim et al. (2024), Geng et al. (2025), and Zhou et al. (2025), and Φt→t−d​(𝐱t)\Phi_{t\rightarrow t-d}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) for Frans et al. (2025). The corresponding task conditioning 𝝉task\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{task}} can thus be boundary-anchored (t→0t\rightarrow 0), interval-conditioned (t→rt\rightarrow r), or step-conditioned (t→t−dt\rightarrow t-d), where the latter two are alternative parameterizations related by r=t−dr=t-d.

For simplicity, we denote the 𝝉task\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{task}}-indexed network as follows, where its output may parameterize the transport map directly or through a velocity or displacement:

fθ​(𝐱t,𝝉task)where𝝉task={t,e.g., consistency models (Song et al., 2023),(t,r),e.g., MeanFlows (Geng et al., 2025),(t,d),e.g., Shortcut Models (Frans et al., 2025).f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t};\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{task}})\quad\text{where}\quad\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{task}}=\begin{cases}t,&\text{e.g., }\text{consistency models \cite[citep]{(\@@bibref{AuthorsPhrase1Year}{song2023consistency}{\@@citephrase{, }}{})}},\\ (t,r),&\text{e.g., }\text{MeanFlows \cite[citep]{(\@@bibref{AuthorsPhrase1Year}{geng2025mean}{\@@citephrase{, }}{})}},\\ (t,d),&\text{e.g., }\text{Shortcut Models \cite[citep]{(\@@bibref{AuthorsPhrase1Year}{frans2025one}{\@@citephrase{, }}{})}}.\end{cases}

Here, 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} denotes the network input, tt the current noise level, rr the desired endpoint time of the transport, and dd the desired step size. Standard diffusion networks are also conditioned on tt, although this conditioning alone does not specify a boundary-anchored transport map.

We contrast these models with methods that lack an explicit time-indexed transport map at inference, e.g., drifting models (Deng et al., 2026), whose objectives constrain the distribution of generated samples without any time-indexed transport task. We use them as negative controls to distinguish generic layerwise refinement from computation organized by a 𝝉task\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{task}}-indexed transport task. We provide additional details on one-step generation in Appendix D.

3 Depth as Time

We introduce depth as time, an empirical observation in which denoising-like structure unfolds across the layers of a one-step generative model. We begin by introducing our methodology for comparing the intermediate temporal outputs of a multi-step flow model with the intermediate layer-wise outputs of a one-step compressed model (Sec. 3.1). We then use this methodology to demonstrate the first evidence of progressive denoising across layers (Sec. 3.2), drawing three conclusions. First, the one-step layers exhibit patterns of denoising, which we call depth as time. Second, the recovered layer-wise mixing schedule in one-step models is different from the standard linear schedule in the temporal progression of multi-step models. Third, we demonstrate that drifting (τ\tau-independent) models do not appear to exhibit depth as time unlike τtask\tau_{\mathrm{task}}-conditioned models such as MeanFlows.

3.1 From sampling time to network depth

Multi-step flow models expose intermediate states across sampling time, whereas one-step generative models expose intermediate representations only across network depth. We therefore introduce a methodology for comparing these two forms of progression.

Consider a multi-step flow model that transports a noisy sample 𝐱t\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}_{t} toward a clean sample 𝐱0\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}_{0} by following a learned velocity field. Flow matching (Lipman et al., 2022, Albergo et al., 2023) defines a probability path between data and noise, e.g., 𝐱t=αt​𝐱0+σt​ϵ\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}_{t}=\alpha_{t}\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}_{0}+\sigma_{t}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}, where ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) and t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1]. Under the linear interpolation considered here, αt=1−t\alpha_{t}=1-t and σt=t\sigma_{t}=t, such that t=0t=0 corresponds to data and t=1t=1 corresponds to noise. Each sampled interpolation has velocity ϵ−𝐱0\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}_{0}, and the corresponding marginal velocity field is 𝒖t​(𝒙)=𝔼⁡[ϵ−𝐱0∣𝐱t=𝒙]\boldsymbol{u}_{t}(\boldsymbol{x})=\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}_{0}\mid\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}_{t}=\boldsymbol{x}]. The model is trained to approximate this field with 𝒗θ​(𝐱t,t)≈𝒖t​(𝐱t)\boldsymbol{v}_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}_{t},t)\approx\boldsymbol{u}_{t}(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}_{t}). Sampling then follows the ODE d​𝐱t/d​t=𝒗θ​(𝐱t,t)d\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}_{t}/dt=\boldsymbol{v}_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}_{t},t), and exposes an explicit sequence of states 𝐱t0,𝐱t1,…,𝐱tK\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{0}},\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{1}},\ldots,\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{K}} across sampling time.

A one-step generator, by contrast, produces its output in a single network call and exposes no such external trajectory. It instead computes a sequence of hidden states 𝐡\mathbf{h} across network depth. Concretely, starting from a noisy input 𝐳=𝐱t\mathbf{z}=\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}_{t} from time step tt, and leveraging the task-conditioning variable 𝝉task{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{task}}} and class conditioning cc, a one-step generator with a dimension-preserving residual stream produces:

𝐡0=𝐄(𝐳),𝐡i+1=𝐁i+1(𝐡i;𝝉task,c),i=0,…,L−1,{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\mathbf{h}_{0}}=\mathbf{E}(\mathbf{z}),\qquad{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\mathbf{h}_{i+1}}=\mathbf{B}_{i+1}\left({\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\mathbf{h}_{i}};{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{task}}},c\right),\qquad i=0,\ldots,L-1, (1)

where 𝐄\mathbf{E} is the input embedding, 𝐁i+1\mathbf{B}_{i+1} denotes the (i+1)(i+1)-th network block, and LL is the total number of blocks. Equivalently, the representation at depth ii is obtained by composing the first ii blocks, 𝐡i=(𝐁i∘⋯∘𝐁1)(𝐡0){\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\mathbf{h}_{i}}=(\mathbf{B}_{i}\circ\cdots\circ\mathbf{B}_{1})({\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\mathbf{h}_{0}}), with the same conditioning supplied to each block. For a velocity-parameterized generator, the model’s final prediction is 𝒗θ​(𝐳,𝝉task,c)=𝐖out​(𝐡L,𝝉task,c)\boldsymbol{v}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z},{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{task}}},c)=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}({\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\mathbf{h}_{L}};\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{task}},c), where 𝐖out\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}} denotes the network head, which includes normalization, adaptive layer normalization modulation (AdaLN), and a linear projection. Depending on the model, this output represents either an instantaneous velocity or an interval-averaged velocity.

Probe. To probe how the model’s prediction develops across depth, we apply the same final head to the hidden state after each block, with the original conditioning and without executing the remaining blocks 𝐁i+1,…,𝐁L\mathbf{B}_{i+1},\ldots,\mathbf{B}_{L}. For layer ii, we define

𝒗i≔𝐖out​(𝐡i,𝝉task,c).\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\boldsymbol{v}_{i}}\coloneqq\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}\left({\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\mathbf{h}_{i}};\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{task}},c\right). (2)

At i=Li=L, this recovers the model’s ordinary output, 𝒗L=𝒗θ​(𝐳,𝝉task,c)\boldsymbol{v}_{L}=\boldsymbol{v}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z},{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{task}}},c). At intermediate layers, 𝒗i\boldsymbol{v}_{i} measures the velocity prediction accessible through the output head from the residual stream at depth ii. This probe introduces no learned parameters and does not modify the generator.11 1 This parameter-free layerwise readout is closely related to the logit lens in language modeling (nostalgebraist, 2020). In Appendix B.1 we demonstrate that similar conclusions can be obtained using a separately trained linear probe, suggesting a lack of reliance on the particular form of the probe, but not by a random untrained probe. Therefore, the observed convergence is semantically meaningful rather than simply numerical.

We then convert each layerwise velocity estimate into the corresponding endpoint prediction. For the linear flow-matching interpolation, the clean-image estimate is 𝐱^0=𝐱t−t​𝒗θ​(𝐱t,t)\hat{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}}_{0}=\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}_{t}-t\,\boldsymbol{v}_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}_{t},t); with the exact marginal velocity field, which recovers the posterior mean 𝔼⁡[𝐱0∣𝐱t]\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}_{0}\mid\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}_{t}]. For an instantaneous velocity prediction, this is a single Euler step, rather than an exact integration of the ODE. For an interval-averaged velocity prediction, it is the model’s finite-interval transport parameterization as in Geng et al. (2025).

Applying this conversion to the layerwise readouts for a one-step input 𝐱t\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}_{t} gives our layerwise endpoint probe,

Simply put, 𝐱~ri{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}}_{r}^{i}} asks what endpoint prediction is already implied by the partially formed residual representation 𝐡i{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\mathbf{h}_{i}} at depth ii. Interestingly, these layerwise velocities 𝒗i{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\boldsymbol{v}_{i}} used to construct 𝐱~ri{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}}_{r}^{i}} have conceptual connections to Neural ODE views of neural networks (Chen et al., 2018) and deep equilibrium models (Bai et al., 2019); we discuss these connections in Appendix A.

3.2 Evidence of progressive denoising across layers

Using the probe methodology of Sec. 3.1, we begin by demonstrating the emergence of depth-as-time in simple toy examples. Specifically, after progressively distilling (Salimans and Ho, 2022) a multi-step 8-Gaussians teacher into a one-step student, we plot the student’s layerwise endpoint predictions 𝐱~0i{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{i}}; for the teacher, we plot 𝐱^0\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0}-predictions for each step along its multi-step sampling trajectory in Figure 1. The teacher 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0}-predictions are external and therefore different from internal layerwise 𝐱~0i{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{i}} predictions. We also plot the normalized distance to the endpoint using Equation (4).

The toy example in Figure 1 exhibits layerwise refinement suggestive of denoising, so we next ask whether this phenomenon extends to large-scale one-step generators. We apply Equation (2) to recent one-step generative models trained with different objectives, including distillation (specifically, latent adversarial distillation for FLUX-schnell (Black Forest Labs et al., 2025)), MeanFlow (Geng et al., 2025), and Drifting (Deng et al., 2026), and visualize the resulting layerwise predictions 𝐱~0i{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{i}} in Figure 2. For MeanFlow and Drifting, we use the released B/2 checkpoints (12 layers, width 768) trained on ImageNet-256×256256\times 256 (Russakovsky et al., 2015).

Qualitatively, FLUX-schnell and MeanFlow (both τtask\tau_{\mathrm{task}}-conditioned models; Sec. 2) exhibit progressive refinement across depth. This progression is also reflected quantitatively by the approximately monotonic decrease in normalized endpoint distance from Equation (4). In contrast, the Drifting model does not exhibit the same systematic depthwise refinement.

In addition to plotting the constructed 𝐱~0i{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{i}} predictions, we also quantify layerwise refinement, by measuring how far each intermediate prediction 𝐱~0i{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{i}} at layer ii (of the clean image 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0}) is from the model’s final prediction 𝐱~0L\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{L}. For a distance or dissimilarity measure dd, we normalize this distance by its maximum along the same trajectory:

𝝆⁡(i)≔d⁡(𝐱~0i,𝐱~0L)max1≤j≤L⁡d⁡(𝐱~0j,𝐱~0L).\boldsymbol{\rho}(i)\coloneqq\frac{d(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{i},\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{L})}{\max_{1\leq j\leq L}d(\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{j},\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{L})}. (4)

We normalize each trajectory separately before averaging across 3232 examples, excluding trajectories for which all distances are zero. In our experiments, we use the ℓ2\ell_{2} distance. Figures 1 and 2 show how distance evolves across intermediate layers in the toy example and for the one-step FLUX model along with their respective teachers.

Recovering an effective mixing schedule. We note that the layerwise refinement observed above, and in particular the normalized distance to the endpoint in Equation (4), is not by itself evidence of denoising. To test whether the layerwise decodes exhibit a denoising-like signal–noise structure, we take inspiration from the probability-path parameterization in Lipman et al. (2022) and solve the inverse problem of recovering depth-dependent mixing coefficients from the layerwise predictions in Figure 2. The intuition is that, if a single pair of coefficients shared across trajectories can explain intermediate predictions as mixtures of the input noise and final prediction, then a denoising-like interpretation of depth is plausible.

We focus on full one-step generation from noisy input to clean output. We recover the coefficients for FLUX-schnell, a MeanFlow B/2 model, and a Shortcut B/2 model (Frans et al., 2025), and contrast these with a τ\tau-independent Drifting B/2 model. Specifically, for depthwise trajectory n{\color[rgb]{0.4648,0.4648,0.4648}n} of each model, we let ϵn\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{{\color[rgb]{0.4648,0.4648,0.4648}n}} denote the input noise and 𝐱~0L,n\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{L,{\color[rgb]{0.4648,0.4648,0.4648}n}} the final generated prediction, and assume

𝐱~0i,n=αi​𝐱~0L,n+σi​ϵn+𝜹in,\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{i,n}={\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\alpha_{i}}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{L,{\color[rgb]{0.4648,0.4648,0.4648}n}}+{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\sigma_{i}}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{{\color[rgb]{0.4648,0.4648,0.4648}n}}+\boldsymbol{\delta}_{i}^{{\color[rgb]{0.4648,0.4648,0.4648}n}}, (5)

where 𝜹in\boldsymbol{\delta}_{i}^{{\color[rgb]{0.4648,0.4648,0.4648}n}} is the unexplained residual. We fit a single pair of coefficients shared across 256 depthwise trajectories at each block: (α^i,σ^i)=arg​minα,σ∑n∈𝒟train∥𝐱~0i,n−α𝐱~0L,n−σϵn∥22{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}(\widehat{\alpha}_{i},\widehat{\sigma}_{i})}=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\alpha,\sigma}\sum_{{\color[rgb]{0.4648,0.4648,0.4648}n}\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}}\|\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{i,{\color[rgb]{0.4648,0.4648,0.4648}n}}-{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\alpha}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{L,{\color[rgb]{0.4648,0.4648,0.4648}n}}-{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\sigma}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{{\color[rgb]{0.4648,0.4648,0.4648}n}}\|_{2}^{2}.

The mapping i↦(α^i,σ^i)i\mapsto{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}(\widehat{\alpha}_{i},\widehat{\sigma}_{i})} defines our effective depthwise mixing schedule. We impose neither monotonicity nor positivity, and we do not enforce the flow-matching constraint αi+σi=1{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\alpha_{i}}+{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\sigma_{i}}=1. Thus, the optimization is unconstrained and any observed difference in the signal and noise coefficients is completely attributed to the depth-as-time trajectories. We evaluate how well the fitted coefficients reconstruct decoded predictions on held-out trajectories in Figure 3.

Across the four models, Drifting stands out as having substantially larger reconstruction residuals between the observed and fitted depthwise trajectories. In fact, its recovered noise coefficient is σi≈0\sigma_{i}\approx 0 at every block (Figure 4), so its intermediate predictions carry no identifiable component of the input noise and do not follow a denoising-like path. In contrast, MeanFlow, FLUX-schnell, and Shortcut are each well described by a two-component signal–noise mixing model despite being trained with different objectives.

Notably, the recovered coefficients do not correspond to a standard flow-matching interpolant, for which αi,σi∈[0,1]\alpha_{i},\sigma_{i}\in[0,1] and αi+σi=1\alpha_{i}+\sigma_{i}=1 along the path. For MeanFlow, for example, we recover α4=2.18\alpha_{4}=2.18 and σ4=−6.04\sigma_{4}=-6.04 at block 4 (Figure 4), with both coefficients outside [0,1][0,1]. Thus, although the low held-out reconstruction error for MeanFlow (≈0.10\approx 0.10 on average across blocks) indicates a recoverable signal–noise organization across depth, the recovered schedule is distinct from the interpolation schedule used during flow-matching training. We interpret this as depth defining its own effective denoising-like coordinate, rather than directly reproducing training time. We provide additional details and recovered schedules for the other models in Appendix B.2.

4 Depth As Time Generalizes to Arbitrary Transport Tasks

Our findings so far show depth as time unfolding across the blocks of a single one-step evaluation that solves the full noise-to-clean task. However, one-step models based on diffusion are trained on a more general transport task that also supports multi-step generation. In this section, we show that depth as time extends to arbitrary start and end points along the generation trajectory, in two settings: distilled models in Sec. 4.1 and MeanFlow in Sec. 4.2 (and relegate Shortcut models to Appendix E.1).

In distilled models, we find that each sampling step contains its own depthwise refinement, nesting depth as time within sampling time. In MeanFlow, the depthwise trajectory adapts to the requested transport interval with an interesting property: when the prescribed endpoint is noisy, intermediate layers first denoise to reveal cleaner structure and then gradually renoise toward that endpoint.

4.1 Distilled one-step generators nest depth as time in sampling time

We first consider distilled one-step models, which are conditioned only on the current state and time fθ​(𝐱t,t)f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t). Because they do not explicitly receive an endpoint rr, multi-step generation relies on an external sampler that uses each network function evaluation (NFE) to advance from the current time tt to a prescribed next time rr. We refer to the resulting transport problem t→rt\rightarrow r as a subtask of the full 1→01\rightarrow 0 generation task.

To probe how computation unfolds within these subtasks, we study two large-scale distilled text-to-image models, FLUX-schnell and SANA-Sprint 0.6B (Chen et al., 2025). For each subtask, we decode both the endpoint prediction 𝐱~ri{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{r}^{i}} and the diagnostic clean prediction 𝐱~0i{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{i}} following Equation (3). The former shows how the layerwise prediction evolves toward the next state prescribed by the sampler; the latter shows what clean image is implied by the same intermediate representation.

Figure 5 shows the layerwise endpoint predictions for FLUX-schnell with generation split into two subtasks, and Figure 6 quantifies both predictions using Equation (4) for FLUX-schnell and SANA-Sprint across four subtasks.

Each subtask exhibits its own depthwise refinement. In Figure 5, the prediction in step 1 sharpens toward a still-noisy intermediate state; step 2 then restarts from that state and refines toward the clean image. In Figure 6, this appears as the 𝐱~ri{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{r}^{i}} curves jumping back up each time the sampler advances. This reset, however, applies only to the sampler state. The diagnostic 𝐱~0i{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{i}} predictions show that even during the first subtask, 1→0.751\rightarrow 0.75, the final layerwise representation already largely implies the clean image at t=0t=0 (Figure 6, second and fourth panels). The amount of refinement in 𝐱~0i{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{i}} also shrinks in later subtasks as the sampler itself approaches the clean endpoint.

The endpoint predictions 𝐱~ri{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{r}^{i}}, by contrast, do not progress as far toward the clean image within each step and can flatten or even reverse within depth, most visibly for FLUX (Figure 6, first panel). This is consistent with the model returning toward the prescribed noisy endpoint. In general, this suggests that sampling time and network depth are distinct but nested axes of progression. We examine the reversal in 𝐱~ri{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{r}^{i}} more directly in explicitly interval-conditioned MeanFlow models in Sec. 4.2.

4.2 MeanFlows Denoise, Then Renoise, Toward Noisy Endpoints

Unlike the distilled models of Sec. 4.1, which receive the endpoint rr only implicitly through the external sampler, MeanFlow (Geng et al., 2025) is explicitly conditioned on the interval (t,r)(t,r) and predicts the average velocity uu over it. This lets us ask directly how the requested endpoint shapes the depthwise trajectory. The probe of Sec. 4.1 carries over directly, except that the final output head now estimates the interval-averaged velocity 𝒖i{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\boldsymbol{u}_{i}} not an instantaneous one. Decoding it gives the layerwise endpoint prediction 𝐱~ri=𝐳t−(t−r)​𝒖i{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{r}^{\,i}}=\mathbf{z}_{t}-(t-r){\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\boldsymbol{u}_{i}} for r>0r>0, and a diagnostic clean-image estimate from the same velocity, 𝐱~0i=𝐳t−t​𝒖i{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{\,i}}=\mathbf{z}_{t}-t{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\boldsymbol{u}_{i}} for r=0r=0.

For one-step generation, the requested endpoint is clean (r=0r=0), and MeanFlow behaves as in Sec. 3.2: on ImageNet (Russakovsky et al., 2015), the layerwise predictions progress approximately monotonically from noise toward the clean image (Figure 2b, top row). Under multi-step sampling, each network evaluation instead solves a subtask t→rt\to r with r>0r>0. The diagnostic clean predictions 𝐱~0i{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{\,i}} show that depth as time persists within each subtask: at every step, the layerwise predictions again progress toward the clean image, nesting depthwise refinement within sampling time as in the distilled models of Sec. 4.1 (Figure 2b, bottom rows).

The endpoint predictions 𝐱~ri{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{r}^{\,i}}, which track what the network actually outputs for each subtask, reveal a different pattern. Because the prescribed endpoint is now noisy, the depthwise trajectory becomes non-monotonic: intermediate layers first reveal a cleaner image structure than the desired target, and later layers gradually renoise the prediction toward 𝐳r\mathbf{z}_{r}. We observe this on both CIFAR-10 (Krizhevsky, 2009) and ImageNet (Figure 2a, top; Figure 2b, middle rows), where the cleanest prediction appears in the intermediate layers (highlighted in red) rather than the noisy endpoint.

The normalized distance ρ⁡(i)\rho(i) for a 5-step MeanFlow on CIFAR-10 quantifies the same effect: within each step, ρ⁡(i)\rho(i) first falls and then rises again before the next step begins (Figure 2a, bottom). We refer to this pattern as denoise-then-renoise. It suggests that even when asked for only a partial transport, the network passes through an estimate of the clean image.

Compositional hypothesis for denoise-then-renoise. At first glance, this trajectory is surprising. An interval-conditioned model is asked to solve the direct transport 𝐳t↦𝐳r\mathbf{z}_{t}\mapsto\mathbf{z}_{r}, yet its intermediate predictions detour through the clean endpoint estimate before returning to the requested noisy one. One candidate explanation is that flow maps satisfy a compositional consistency property (Boffi et al., 2025) (or a one-parameteric semigroup). Writing Φt→r\Phi_{t\rightarrow r} for the transport from time tt to time rr, any intermediate time ss gives Φt→r=Φs→r∘Φt→s\Phi_{t\rightarrow r}=\Phi_{s\rightarrow r}\circ\Phi_{t\rightarrow s}. Composing through the clean boundary, in particular, yields Φt→r​(𝐳t)=Φ0→r​(Φt→0​(𝐳t))\Phi_{t\rightarrow r}(\mathbf{z}_{t})=\Phi_{0\rightarrow r}\!\left(\Phi_{t\rightarrow 0}(\mathbf{z}_{t})\right), a factorization 𝐳t→𝐳0→𝐳r\mathbf{z}_{t}\rightarrow\mathbf{z}_{0}\rightarrow\mathbf{z}_{r} that matches the observed trajectory. Yet, compositional consistency alone cannot be the full explanation since it holds equally for every intermediate time ss and therefore does not single out the clean endpoint.

The clean endpoint estimate is instead singled out by the structure of the training target. For example, under the linear path 𝐳t=(1−t)​𝐱0+t​ϵ\mathbf{z}_{t}=(1-t)\mathbf{x}_{0}+t\epsilon, the marginal velocity is affine in the posterior clean estimate: v⁡(𝐳t,t)=𝔼⁡[ϵ−𝐱0∣𝐳t]=𝐳t−𝔼⁡[𝐱0∣𝐳t]tv(\mathbf{z}_{t},t)=\mathbb{E}[\epsilon-\mathbf{x}_{0}\mid\mathbf{z}_{t}]=\frac{\mathbf{z}_{t}-{\color[rgb]{0.1172,0.3047,0.5508}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_{0}\mid\mathbf{z}_{t}]}}{t} (Lipman et al., 2022, Albergo et al., 2023)33 3 The same holds for any affine path 𝐳t=αt​𝐱0+σt​ϵ\mathbf{z}_{t}=\alpha_{t}\mathbf{x}_{0}+\sigma_{t}\epsilon, since 𝔼⁡[ϵ∣𝐳t]=(𝐳t−αt​𝔼​[𝐱0∣𝐳t])/σt\mathbb{E}[\epsilon\mid\mathbf{z}_{t}]=\big(\mathbf{z}_{t}-\alpha_{t}{\color[rgb]{0.1172,0.3047,0.5508}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_{0}\mid\mathbf{z}_{t}]}\big)/\sigma_{t}.. A single Euler step to any endpoint rr therefore gives 𝐳t−(t−r)​v​(𝐳t,t)=rt​𝐳t+(1−rt)​𝔼​[𝐱0∣𝐳t]\mathbf{z}_{t}-(t-r)\,v(\mathbf{z}_{t},t)=\tfrac{r}{t}\mathbf{z}_{t}+\left(1-\tfrac{r}{t}\right){\color[rgb]{0.1172,0.3047,0.5508}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_{0}\mid\mathbf{z}_{t}]}, so every endpoint estimate with r<tr<t is an affine combination of 𝐳t\mathbf{z}_{t} and 𝔼⁡[𝐱0∣𝐳t]{\color[rgb]{0.1172,0.3047,0.5508}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_{0}\mid\mathbf{z}_{t}]}. The posterior clean estimate is thus a non-trivial computation shared across all of these tasks.

For MeanFlow, this extends beyond a single Euler step: the average velocity u⁡(𝐳t,t,r)=1t−r​∫rtv⁡(𝐳s,s)​𝑑su(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,r)=\frac{1}{t-r}\int_{r}^{t}v(\mathbf{z}_{s},s)\,ds satisfies the MeanFlow identity: u⁡(𝐳t,t,r)=v⁡(𝐳t,t)−(t−r)​dd​t​u​(𝐳t,t,r)u(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,r)=v(\mathbf{z}_{t},t)-(t-r)\,\frac{d}{dt}u(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,r) (Geng et al., 2025). The first term, v⁡(𝐳t,t)v(\mathbf{z}_{t},t), is independent of rr and, determined by the clean estimate 𝔼⁡[𝐱0∣𝐳t]{\color[rgb]{0.1172,0.3047,0.5508}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_{0}\mid\mathbf{z}_{t}]}; the second is an interval-dependent correction that vanishes as r→tr\rightarrow t. Therefore, a network trained jointly over many (t,r)(t,r) pairs has a natural computation to reuse: first resolve the clean sample implied by 𝐳t\mathbf{z}_{t}, then apply the rr-specific correction that carries it to the requested endpoint. This two-stage computation matches the observed denoise-then-renoise trajectory in Figure 2.

5 Making Depth as Time Explicit

So far we demonstrated that task-conditioned one-step models refine their predictions across layers in a denoising-like manner. A natural next question is whether this layerwise computation can itself be explicitly modeled as a flow, with a single weight-shared block applied repeatedly and conditioned on a time variable that loosely corresponds to the layer index. If so, the one-step model could be compressed further in its number of parameters, while also gaining the flexibility to vary the number of depthwise steps rather than being tied to a fixed number of layers LL.

Concretely, the one-step model has a sequence of layer-specific blocks {𝐁i}i=1L\{\mathbf{B}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{L}, with hidden layers 𝐡i+1=𝐁i+1​(𝐡i,𝝉task,c)\mathbf{h}_{i+1}=\mathbf{B}_{i+1}(\mathbf{h}_{i};\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{task}},c) (eq. 1). We have demonstrated that these blocks loosely correspond to denoising via depth as time. Making this explicit, we can rewrite the model as:

𝐡τi+1=𝐁θ​(𝐡τi,(τi,τi+1),𝝉task,c),\mathbf{h}_{\tau_{i+1}}={\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\mathbf{B}_{\theta}}\left(\mathbf{h}_{\tau_{i}},{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}(\tau_{i},\tau_{i+1})};{\color[rgb]{0.4648,0.4648,0.4648}\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{task}},c}\right), (6)

with the time interval conditioning (τi,τi+1){\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}(\tau_{i},\tau_{i+1})} replacing the layer-specific transformations. Intuitively, we can view this sequence as a flow in the representation space: each application of 𝐁θ{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\mathbf{B}_{\theta}} over the computational interval (τi,τi+1)(\tau_{i},\tau_{i+1}) transports the hidden state 𝐡τi\mathbf{h}_{\tau_{i}} to 𝐡τi+1\mathbf{h}_{\tau_{i+1}}. If we set τi=i/L{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\tau_{i}}=i/L, we maintain LL steps corresponding to the LL layers.

We train the parameters 𝐁θ\mathbf{B}_{\theta} using the supervision signal from the LL hidden layers 𝐡1,…,𝐡L\mathbf{h}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{h}_{L} of the one-step model. We embed the conditioning variables, including the interval (τi,τi+1)(\tau_{i},\tau_{i+1}), and inject them into the shared block through adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN) modulation. This training is data-free and uses only random noise z∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)z\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}), sampled class labels, and the one-step teacher model representations. See Appendix C.1 for training details.

Parameter compression. Using this formulation, we compress the MeanFlow SiT-B/2 and SiT-L/2 one-step models for ImageNet 256×256256{\times}256 from 131131M and 459459M to 16.016.0M and 27.627.6M parameters, respectively, corresponding to 8.2×8.2\times and 16.6×16.6\times compression. The compressed models reach FID-50k 15.615.6 and 11.711.7, which improve to 8.28.2 and 4.94.9 with FD-loss post-training (Yang et al., 2026), compared with 6.26.2 and 4.04.0 for the original models. Using two unique blocks instead of one trades some compression for quality, reaching FID 5.845.84 with 26.626.6M parameters (4.9×4.9\times compression) for SiT-B/2 and 4.044.04 with 46.546.5M parameters (9.9×9.9\times) for SiT-L/2 after post-training. We ablate the effect of conditioning on the interval (τi,τi+1)(\tau_{i},\tau_{i+1}) in Appendix C.4 and show that on CIFAR-10, removing it from an otherwise identical weight-shared block more than doubles FID-50k.

Compute compression. Because 𝐁θ\mathbf{B}_{\theta} now defines a flow over depth, we can also borrow intuition from accelerating diffusion models to reduce inference-time compute, training over coarse intervals (τa,τb)(\tau_{a},\tau_{b}) that span multiple layers so that 𝐁θ\mathbf{B}_{\theta} runs fewer than LL times. For SiT-L/2 with two unique blocks, halving the number of block applications gives FID 5.255.25, and reducing it by 3×3\times gives 6.116.11, against a teacher FID of 4.014.01 (after post-training). In contrast, simply running the native-depth student with fewer applications degrades FID (Appendix C.3). Much like sampling steps in diffusion, the number of depthwise steps thus becomes a knob that trades compute for quality within a single forward pass.

MeanFlow models are more compressible than drifting models. Finally, recall that drifting models, which lack a time-indexed transport task or training signal, do not exhibit depth as time (Sec. 3.2), even though their predictions still sharpen in later blocks. Consistent with this, making depth as time explicit fails for them: with an analogous procedure (Appendix C.5), the drifting B/2 student reaches only FID-50k 47.0947.09, about three times worse than the MeanFlow SiT-B/2 student (15.6115.61) at a similar compression ratio, despite distilling from a stronger teacher (FID 1.751.75). It therefore seems that refinement along depth is not enough to result in a compressible one-step generator, and that the time-indexed transport task is what organizes this refinement into a denoising process compact enough for a single time-conditioned block.

Full training details and results are in Appendix C.

6 Conclusion

We began by asking what happens to the denoising trajectory of diffusion when generation is compressed into a single forward pass. Through a series of experiments, we showed that one-step generative models exhibit a denoising-like progression across network depth, a phenomenon we call depth as time. Decoding intermediate representations further revealed that this progression reflects the transport task being solved, from approximately monotonic denoising toward clean endpoints to denoise-then-renoise when the prescribed endpoint remains noisy. Finally, we made this depthwise structure explicit and reveal that models with explicit time-indexed transport maps are more compressible. Leveraging this property with weight sharing and coarse depthwise steps, we can further compress both parameters and compute, resulting in a more compute efficient one-step model.

Appendix A Related Work and Discussion

This appendix expands the related work in the main text. Multi-step generators compute across network calls in sampling time, while a one-step generator computes across the layers of a single forward pass. We ask how the former is reorganized into the latter, and whether the resulting depthwise trajectory can itself be modeled and compressed as a flow.

Depth as a dynamical process.

Neural ODEs (Chen et al., 2018) view a residual update 𝐡i+1=𝐡i+g⁡(𝐡i)\mathbf{h}_{i+1}=\mathbf{h}_{i}+g(\mathbf{h}_{i}) as an Euler step, with depth playing the role of time. Our layerwise predictions 𝒗i=𝐖out​(𝐡i,𝝉task,c)\boldsymbol{v}_{i}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}(\mathbf{h}_{i};\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{task}},c), obtained by applying the model’s output layer (normalization, AdaLN modulation, and linear projection) to each intermediate state, make this view measurable in generative models. Universal Transformers (Dehghani et al., 2019) apply one shared block repeatedly with a per-step timestep embedding, the closest precedent for our explicit model (Section 5); our block is instead conditioned on an interval (τa,τb)(\tau_{a},\tau_{b}) of an internal clock, which allows steps of different sizes. DiffusionBlocks (Shing et al., 2026) treats residual blocks as denoising steps by design, assigning each block a range of noise levels so that blocks can be trained independently; we find that this correspondence already emerges in one-step generators trained end-to-end. Deep equilibrium models (Bai et al., 2019, Anil et al., 2022) and related implicit models (Geng et al., 2021a, Geng et al., 2021b, Fung et al., 2022, Gu et al., 2020, Labovich, 2026) define the representation as a fixed point 𝐳⋆=fθ​(𝐳⋆,𝐱)\mathbf{z}^{\star}=f_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}^{\star};\mathbf{x}).

Layerwise predictions and probing.

Computing layerwise predictions with the model’s own output layer is the generative analogue of the logit lens (nostalgebraist, 2020), which decodes the intermediate states of language models with the unembedding and reveals a gradual refinement toward the final prediction. Because what such decodings reveal can depend strongly on the layer and on the choice of decoder (Lu et al., 2025), we confirm our results with a trained and a random linear probe (Appendix B.1). Representations of diffusion models have mostly been studied across sampling time (Li et al., 2023, Clark and Jaini, 2023); we study them across depth within a single evaluation.

Depth as iterative refinement.

Depth often implements incremental refinement rather than distinct transformations (Liu et al., 2026, Pappone et al., 2025). We find that in one-step generators this refinement is shaped by the transport task: it follows a denoising-like schedule (Section 3.2), adapts to the requested endpoint (Section 4.2), and, unlike in drifting models, can be compressed into a single time-conditioned block (Section 5, Appendix C.5).

Weight-tied and looped computation.

Weight tying decouples computation from parameters. Looped Transformers can emulate programmable computers (Giannou et al., 2023), learn iterative algorithms (Yang et al., 2024), match deeper models (Saunshi et al., 2025), and extrapolate to more iterations than seen in training (Kohli et al., 2026), though an extra iteration is worth less than an extra layer (Schwethelm et al., 2026). Timestep encodings recover iteration-dependent behavior in looped models (Xu and Sato, 2025), and our internal clock plays this role for generation (Appendix C.4).

One-step generative models.

One-step generators are obtained by distilling a multi-step teacher (Salimans and Ho, 2022, Luo et al., 2023, Yin et al., 2024, Zhou et al., 2024, Sauer et al., 2024a, Sauer et al., 2024b) or by learning flow maps directly (Song et al., 2023, Kim et al., 2024, Frans et al., 2025, Boffi et al., 2025, Geng et al., 2025, Zhou et al., 2025), while GANs (Goodfellow et al., 2014) and drifting models (Deng et al., 2026) match only the output distribution (Appendix D). These methods compress sampling time; we ask where that computation goes, and show that it can be compressed further across depth.

Appendix B Readout Controls and Depthwise mixing details

B.1 Readout Controls

A natural concern is that the endpoint-convergence pattern measured by Eq. (4) may be an artifact of applying the model’s final readout 𝐖out\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}} to intermediate residual states. Since this readout is optimized only for the final representation 𝐡L{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\mathbf{h}_{L}}, intermediate states might gradually become more compatible with it regardless of whether they encode anything meaningful. To assess how the pattern depends on the readout, we compare 𝐖out\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}} with a trained and a random linear probe.

Trained probe. We fit an independent linear map 𝐕\mathbf{V} by closed-form ridge regression on the layer-normalized final hidden state, such that 𝐕⁡(LayerNorm⁡(𝐡L))≈𝐖out​(𝐡L).\mathbf{V}\bigl(\mathrm{LayerNorm}({\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\mathbf{h}_{L}})\bigr)\approx\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}\bigl({\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\mathbf{h}_{L}}\bigr). The target is the model’s own final prediction, which may be a velocity 𝒗\boldsymbol{v}, noise ϵ\boldsymbol{\epsilon}, or image 𝐱\boldsymbol{\mathbf{x}}. We then freeze 𝐕\mathbf{V} and apply it to every intermediate hidden state 𝐡i{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\mathbf{h}_{i}}; the probe is never trained on intermediate layers. On one-step FLUX-schnell, the trained probe traces nearly the same trajectory as 𝐖out\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}} (Fig. 8), indicating that the pattern does not depend on the particular form of the readout.

Random probe. We also evaluate a frozen random linear map with the same input and output dimensions as 𝐕\mathbf{V}. We sample 𝐕rand∼𝒩​(0,1)D×dout\mathbf{V}_{\mathrm{rand}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)^{D\times d_{\mathrm{out}}} and rescale its weights to match the entrywise standard deviation of 𝐕\mathbf{V}. At each layer, we compute 𝒗irand=𝐕rand​(LayerNorm⁡(𝐡i)),\boldsymbol{v}_{i}^{\mathrm{rand}}=\mathbf{V}_{\mathrm{rand}}\bigl(\mathrm{LayerNorm}({\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\mathbf{h}_{i}})\bigr), without training the probe to match the model’s predictions. The random probe does not reproduce the convergence pattern (Fig. 8): its ρ⁡(i)\rho(i) stays close to 11 through nearly all blocks and drops only in the last few, where it reaches zero simply because each trajectory is normalized to its own endpoint. The progressive convergence observed with 𝐖out\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}} is therefore semantically meaningful rather than a numerical artifact of applying any linear map.

B.2 Depthwise Mixing Details

Mixing model. For trajectory nn, let ϵn\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{n} be the Gaussian input latent and 𝐱~0L,n\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{L,n} the model’s final endpoint prediction. At each block ii, we fit one coefficient pair (αi,σi)(\alpha_{i},\sigma_{i}), shared across trajectories, by unconstrained least squares over all spatial and latent dimensions:

𝐱~0i,n≈αi​𝐱~0L,n+σi​ϵn.\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{i,n}\;\approx\;\alpha_{i}\,\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{L,n}+\sigma_{i}\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{n}.

Coefficients are fit on a training split, and for i<Li<L we report the held-out reconstruction error

Ri=∑n‖𝐱~0i,n−α^i​𝐱~0L,n−σ^i​ϵn‖22∑n‖𝐱~0i,n−𝐱~0L,n‖22,R_{i}=\frac{\sum_{n}\big\|\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{i,n}-\widehat{\alpha}_{i}\,\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{L,n}-\widehat{\sigma}_{i}\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{n}\big\|_{2}^{2}}{\sum_{n}\big\|\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{i,n}-\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{L,n}\big\|_{2}^{2}},

normalized by the error of predicting the final output directly, so that Ri=1R_{i}=1 means no improvement over this baseline.

Setup. We analyze MeanFlow B/2 (L=12L=12), Drifting B/2 (L=12L=12), FLUX-schnell (single-stream blocks, L=38L=38), SANA-Sprint (L=28L=28), and Shortcut B/2 (L=12L=12). For each, we extract N=256N=256 trajectories from a single network evaluation with a fixed seed and split them 70/3070/30 into 179179 training and 7777 held-out trajectories.

Results. For the four task-conditioned models, σi\sigma_{i} rises from strongly negative values toward zero across depth while αi\alpha_{i} remains of order one (Figure 9), a systematic signal–noise mixing structure. For MeanFlow, this structure is fit with low held-out error (mean R≈0.10R\approx 0.10), and its coefficients extend well outside the [0,1][0,1] range of a flow-matching interpolant, so depth follows its own effective schedule. For Drifting, σi≈0\sigma_{i}\approx 0 at every block, so the input noise plays no identifiable role, and the fit is substantially worse (mean R≈0.47R\approx 0.47).

Normalization control. MeanFlow’s readout uses LayerNorm, which centers its input, whereas Drifting’s uses RMSNorm, which does not, so centering could in principle induce the mixing structure. We therefore swap only the normalization, keeping the trained AdaLN modulation and linear projection: we remove centering from MeanFlow and add it to Drifting, then refit the coefficients (N=192N=192, same protocol). Removing centering leaves MeanFlow’s RiR_{i} essentially unchanged, and adding it to Drifting makes the fit marginally worse (Figure 10), so the contrast is not an artifact of normalization.

Appendix C Implementation Details for Making Depth as Time Explicit

Here, we provide the details behind Section 5. We first describe how the weight-shared block 𝐁θ\mathbf{B}_{\theta} is trained by distilling the depthwise trajectory of a one-step teacher, and how it is trained and run with coarser steps at inference (App. C.1). We then describe FD-loss post-training (App. C.2) and report full results for parameter and compute compression, including qualitative samples (App. C.3). Finally, we ablate the internal clock on CIFAR-10 (App. C.4) and detail the drifting control (App. C.5).

C.1 Distilling the depthwise trajectory

Architecture. The student replaces the LL layer-specific blocks of a one-step MeanFlow teacher (SiT-B/2, L=12L=12; SiT-L/2, L=24L=24) with n∈{1,2}n\in\{1,2\} unique blocks, applied in alternation for KK steps. Each application is conditioned on its interval of the internal clock (τa,τb)(\tau_{a},\tau_{b}), together with the task conditioning 𝝉task=(t,r)=(1,0)\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{task}}=(t,r)=(1,0) for one-step generation and the class label cc, all injected through AdaLN modulation. The input embedding 𝐄\mathbf{E} and output readout 𝐖out\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}} are copied from the teacher and kept frozen, so only the shared blocks and the clock embedding are trained. The shared blocks are warm-started from the teacher’s middle block.

Objective. Let {𝐇j}j=1L\{\mathbf{H}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{L} denote the teacher’s hidden states for an input 𝐳∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) and label cc. A student with KK applications uses stride s=L/Ks=L/{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}K}, and the state 𝐡k\mathbf{h}_{k} reached after its kk-th application is trained to match the teacher state 𝐇k​s\mathbf{H}_{ks}. Because the norms of the teacher’s hidden states grow with depth, an unnormalized loss would be dominated by the last layers and effectively ignore early ones, so we normalize each term by the norm of its teacher state. We additionally anchor the final decoded prediction to the teacher’s one-step sample 𝐱0T\mathbf{x}_{0}^{T}:

ℒcomp​(θ)=𝔼𝐳,c​[1K​∑k=1K‖𝐡k−𝐇k​s‖22‖𝐇k​s‖22+λ​‖(𝐳−𝒗)−𝐱0T‖22],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{comp}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z},c}\!\left[\frac{1}{{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}K}}\sum_{k=1}^{{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}K}}\frac{\|\mathbf{h}_{k}-\mathbf{H}_{ks}\|_{2}^{2}}{\|\mathbf{H}_{ks}\|_{2}^{2}}+\lambda\,\big\|(\mathbf{z}-\boldsymbol{v})-\mathbf{x}_{0}^{T}\big\|_{2}^{2}\right], (7)

where 𝒗=𝐖out​(𝐡K,𝝉task,c)\boldsymbol{v}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}(\mathbf{h}_{{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}K}};\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{task}},c) is decoded from the final student state and λ=1\lambda=1. Since the teacher provides its full deterministic trajectory, no self-consistency objective is required, and training is data-free: it uses only noise 𝐳∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈)\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) and sampled class labels, which are replaced by the null label with probability punc=0.1p_{\mathrm{unc}}=0.1 to support classifier-free guidance (CFG).

Fixed-KK and elastic training. A fixed-KK student is trained for a single number of applications (Alg. C.1). An elastic student samples KK uniformly from a set 𝒦\mathcal{K} at every iteration (Alg. C.2), so that one model can be run at any depth in the set; we use 𝒦={2,4,6,12}\mathcal{K}=\{2,4,6,12\} for B/2 and 𝒦={4,6,8,12,24}\mathcal{K}=\{4,6,8,12,24\} for L/2. The parameter-compression models in Section 5 are fixed-KK students with K=LK=L, so that s=1s=1 and every teacher state is supervised. When K<LK<L, a few applications over coarse intervals replace several fine-grained transitions along depth (Fig. 11).

Hyperparameters. All fixed-KK students, for both B/2 and L/2 and every number of unique blocks, are trained for 1.21.2M iterations with batch size 3232, learning rate 10−410^{-4} with 2,0002{,}000 warmup steps, and EMA decay 0.99990.9999. The elastic students use the same settings.

Inference and compute accounting. Alg. C.3 generates a sample by running the student for KK applications and decoding once with 𝐖out\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}. With CFG, this is done twice. All FLOPs in Table 2 are reported relative to the same student at its native depth K=LK=L, with CFG in both cases. Note that the MeanFlow teacher incorporates guidance into training and is evaluated with a single pass (ω=1\omega=1), so a student at its native depth costs roughly twice the teacher per sample.

C.2 FD-loss post-training

After distillation, we optionally fine-tune each student with the FD loss of Yang et al. (2026), which backpropagates directly through the Fréchet distance between generated and real feature statistics rather than through a per-sample loss. We compute the distance jointly in three feature spaces, SigLIP, Inception, and MAE, each normalized so that no single space dominates, against precomputed moments of real ImageNet features. The population moments of generated features are tracked with an EMA of decay 0.9990.999. We fine-tune for 20,00020{,}000 steps with learning rate 10−610^{-6} and effective batch size 3232 (4×84\times 8 gradient accumulation), keeping the CFG scale fixed at the optimum of the distilled model. Unlike distillation, this stage uses statistics of real data.

C.3 Results

Parameter compression. Table 1 reports all fixed-KK students at the teacher’s depth. Adding unique blocks improves FID at the cost of less compression: for B/2, pre-FD FID improves from 15.6115.61 with one block to 12.4312.43 with two. FD-loss post-training improves every model by 33–7.57.5 FID, with larger gains for weaker starting models. Figure 12 places these models among existing one-step generators, and Figures 15–17 show paired samples from the SiT-L/2 teacher and its students.

Compute compression. Table 2 reports FID after FD-loss post-training as the number of block applications decreases, for two-block students; Table 3 gives the corresponding pre-FD numbers for the elastic models, and Figure 13 plots both. Three observations stand out. First, a model trained at its native depth cannot simply be run with fewer, coarser applications: probing the native-depth model below its training depth collapses to FID above 290290. Second, students trained for coarse intervals degrade gracefully, especially at larger scale: the L/2 fixed-KK student reaches FID 5.255.25 with half the block applications and 6.116.11 with a third, against a teacher FID of 4.014.01. Third, a single elastic model tracks the separately trained fixed-KK models closely at moderate compression (e.g., 6.136.13 vs. 6.116.11 for L/2 at K=8K=8), but falls behind at the most aggressive setting.

C.4 Ablating the internal time conditioning

To test whether the benefit of weight sharing comes from treating depth as time, we compare two weight-tied models that differ only in whether they receive the internal clock. No publicly released DiT-based MeanFlow model exists for CIFAR-10 to distill from, so both are trained from scratch with the MeanFlow (t,r)(t,r) objective; the CIFAR-10 MeanFlow model analyzed in Fig. 2 is likewise our own.

Setup. Both models use a DiT-B/2 backbone (hidden size 768768, 1212 heads, patch size 22), class conditioning over the 1010 CIFAR-10 classes with label dropout 0.10.1, and EMA decay 0.99990.9999, and both are trained for 400400k iterations. We compare (i) a single tied block applied K=20K=20 times with the internal clock, and (ii) the identical architecture with the clock removed from the AdaLN modulation, so that the block acts identically at every step. Samples are generated in one step (t=1t=1, r=0r=0) without guidance, and FID is computed against CIFAR-10 training-set statistics.

Results. Removing the clock from the tied block more than doubles FID-50k (21.27→45.4521.27\to 45.45; Table 4). Weight tying therefore works only when each application is told where it is along the computational trajectory.

C.5 Drifting models as a negative control

Drifting models (Deng et al., 2026) constrain the endpoint distribution without prescribing a time-indexed transport task. Although they can still refine their predictions over depth, their intermediate residual states do not form the same readable trajectory under the model’s own 𝐖out\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}} readout; recognizable structure emerges primarily in later blocks (Fig. 14).

Distillation recipe. We distill the latent-space drifting DiT-B/2 (1212 blocks, hidden size 768768, 1212 heads, 1616 register tokens) into a single tied block with K=12K=12 and the internal clock. The recipe follows the MeanFlow one with two differences. First, because the norm of the teacher’s residual stream grows by roughly 141.5×141.5\times across depth (as opposed to MeanFlow’s 22.9×22.9\times), we match ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalized states, supervising their direction. Second, because drifting models have no transport conditioning, the student receives only the class label and the interval (τi,τi+1)(\tau_{i},\tau_{i+1}), and its output head predicts the image directly.

Results. As Table 5 shows, this procedure does not produce an effective compressed drifting model: at a similar compression ratio, the drifting student reaches FID 47.0947.09, about three times worse than the MeanFlow student (15.6115.61).

Appendix D Extra Background on One-Step Generators

This appendix reviews the training objectives of the one-step generators analyzed in the main paper, following the taxonomy of Section 2. We first cover distillation, where a one-step student is trained against a multi-step teacher (App. D.1). We then cover flow maps trained with self-consistency objectives, both boundary-anchored and interval-conditioned (App. D.2), and step-conditioned (App. D.3). Throughout, we use the convention of Section 3.1: 𝐱t=(1−t)​𝐱0+t​ϵ\mathbf{x}_{t}=(1-t)\mathbf{x}_{0}+t\boldsymbol{\epsilon}, so that t=0t=0 corresponds to data and t=1t=1 to noise, with instantaneous velocity v⁡(𝐱t,t)v(\mathbf{x}_{t},t) and flow map Φt→r​(𝐱t)≔𝐱t−∫rtv⁡(𝐱τ,τ)​𝑑τ\Phi_{t\to r}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\coloneqq\mathbf{x}_{t}-\int_{r}^{t}v(\mathbf{x}_{\tau},\tau)\,d\tau.

D.1 Distillation

Distillation methods train a one-step generator Gθ​(z)G_{\theta}(z) to reproduce the output distribution of a multi-step teacher. A representative example is distribution matching distillation (DMD) (Yin et al., 2024), commonly expressed as a reverse KL divergence between the noised student and teacher distributions, ℒDMD​(θ)≔𝔼t​[ω⁡(t)​𝔼𝐱tθ∼ptθ​[log⁡ptθ​(𝐱tθ)−log⁡pt​(𝐱tθ)]],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DMD}}(\theta)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}_{t}\!\left[\omega(t)\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{t}^{\theta}\sim p_{t}^{\theta}}\!\left[\log p_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{\theta})-\log p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{\theta})\right]\right], where ω⁡(t)\omega(t) is a time-dependent weighting function. The distributions ptp_{t} and ptθp_{t}^{\theta} use the same Gaussian perturbation kernel pt​(𝐱t∣𝐱0)p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{0}) but differ in their clean-data distributions: pdatap_{\mathrm{data}} for real samples and p0θp_{0}^{\theta} for samples produced by the student. The optimum is attained when p0θ∗=pdatap_{0}^{\theta^{*}}=p_{\mathrm{data}}. Because neither log⁡pt\log p_{t} nor log⁡ptθ\log p_{t}^{\theta} is available in closed form, DMD estimates the generator gradient from the difference between real and fake score functions,

∇θℒDMD=𝔼z,t,ϵ​[ω⁡(t)​(sfake​(𝐱tθ,t)−sreal​(𝐱tθ,t))⊤​∂Gθ​(z)∂θ],\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DMD}}=\mathbb{E}_{z,\,t,\,\epsilon}\!\left[{\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}\omega(t)}\,{\color[rgb]{0.1172,0.3047,0.5508}\big(s_{\mathrm{fake}}(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{\theta},t)-s_{\mathrm{real}}(\mathbf{x}_{t}^{\theta},t)\big)^{\!\top}}\,{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\frac{\partial G_{\theta}(z)}{\partial\theta}}\right], (8)

where 𝐱tθ=αt​Gθ​(z)+σt​ϵ\mathbf{x}_{t}^{\theta}=\alpha_{t}G_{\theta}(z)+\sigma_{t}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}. Here, sreals_{\mathrm{real}} and sfakes_{\mathrm{fake}} estimate the scores of ptp_{t} and ptθp_{t}^{\theta}, respectively, and sfakes_{\mathrm{fake}} is detached when differentiating the generator. The score difference sfake−sreals_{\mathrm{fake}}-s_{\mathrm{real}} is contracted with the student Jacobian ∂Gθ/∂θ\partial G_{\theta}/\partial\theta, supervising the student across noise levels tt.

The distilled models we analyze use related objectives. FLUX-schnell is trained with latent adversarial diffusion distillation (LADD) (Sauer et al., 2024a), whose discriminator operates on noised samples at varying diffusion times, and SANA-Sprint (Chen et al., 2025) combines a continuous-time consistency objective with LADD. Although these methods match distributions rather than explicitly reproducing the teacher’s sampling trajectory, their learning signal remains indexed by diffusion time. This is one reason to expect their students to organize computation along a denoising-like trajectory across depth, as we observe in Sections 3 and 4.1.

D.2 Boundary-anchored and interval-conditioned flow maps

Consistency models (Song et al., 2023) learn a flow map whose endpoint is fixed to the clean sample, fθ​(𝐱t,t)≈Φt→0​(𝐱t)f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t)\approx\Phi_{t\to 0}(\mathbf{x}_{t}). Subsequent work lifts this restriction and learns transport between arbitrary pairs of times tt and rr. Consistency trajectory models (CTM) (Kim et al., 2024) and MeanFlow (MF) (Geng et al., 2025) are two instances of this more general formulation.

Parameterization. CTM parameterizes the map from tt to rr with a displacement gθg_{\theta}, whereas MeanFlow parameterizes the same transport with an interval-averaged velocity uθ​(𝐱t,t,r)≈1t−r​∫rtv⁡(𝐱τ,τ)​𝑑τu_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,r)\approx\frac{1}{t-r}\int_{r}^{t}v(\mathbf{x}_{\tau},\tau)\,d\tau. Both approximate the flow map:

Φt→r​(𝐱t)≈rt​𝐱t+t−rt​gθ​(𝐱t,t,r)⏟CTM=𝐱t−(t−r)​uθ​(𝐱t,t,r)⏟MF,\Phi_{t\to r}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\approx\underbrace{\tfrac{r}{t}\,\mathbf{x}_{t}+\tfrac{t-r}{t}\,g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,r)}_{\mathrm{CTM}}=\underbrace{\mathbf{x}_{t}-(t-r)\,u_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,r)}_{\mathrm{MF}}, (9)

mapping the current state 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} to the endpoint 𝐱r\mathbf{x}_{r}.44 4 We refer the reader to Chapter 11 of Lai et al. (2025) for a detailed relationship between the two parameterizations.

Training. Both methods construct their targets largely from the model’s own predictions. Writing Gθ​(𝐱t,t,r)G_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,r) for CTM’s estimate of Φt→r​(𝐱t)\Phi_{t\to r}(\mathbf{x}_{t}), CTM enforces self-consistency by requiring a direct map from tt to rr to agree with one that passes through an intermediate time s∈[r,t]s\in[r,t], ℒCTM​(θ)=𝔼t,s,r​𝔼𝐱t∼pt​[‖Gθ​(𝐱t,t,r)−Gθ−​(Φ^t→s​(𝐱t),s,r)‖22],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CTM}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t,s,r}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{t}\sim p_{t}}\!\left[\left\|G_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,r)-G_{\theta^{-}}\!\left(\hat{\Phi}_{t\to s}(\mathbf{x}_{t}),s,r\right)\right\|_{2}^{2}\right], where Φ^t→s\hat{\Phi}_{t\to s} is obtained by numerically solving a pretrained teacher’s ODE from tt to ss, and θ−\theta^{-} denotes detached parameters. MeanFlow instead trains the interval-averaged velocity using the instantaneous velocity together with a correction involving the total derivative of the interval average, ℒMF​(θ)=𝔼t,r​𝔼𝐱t∼pt​[‖uθ​(𝐱t,t,r)−sg⁡(v⁡(𝐱t,t)−(t−r)​dd​t​uθ​(𝐱t,t,r))‖22],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MF}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t,r}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{t}\sim p_{t}}\!\left[\left\|u_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,r)-\mathrm{sg}\!\left(v(\mathbf{x}_{t},t)-(t-r)\frac{d}{dt}u_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,r)\right)\right\|_{2}^{2}\right], where sg⁡(⋅)\mathrm{sg}(\cdot) denotes the stop-gradient operator.

Clean versus interval endpoints. The distinction between clean-endpoint and interval-endpoint prediction is central to the depthwise behavior we observe. When r=0r=0, the model transports 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} directly to the clean sample 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0}. In a multi-step flow map, however, rr may be greater than zero, so the target 𝐱r\mathbf{x}_{r} remains a noisy intermediate state. MeanFlow is therefore trained to predict an average velocity anchored to the interval endpoint 𝐱r\mathbf{x}_{r}, rather than always to the clean image 𝐱0\mathbf{x}_{0}. As we show in Section 4.2, this difference in the training objective changes the structure of the trajectory across depth, producing the denoise-then-renoise pattern.

D.3 Step-conditioned flow maps: Shortcut models

Shortcut models (Frans et al., 2025) condition the network not only on the current time tt but also on a desired step size dd. The model learns a shortcut sθ​(𝐱t,t,d)s_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,d) that transports 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} to the state a distance dd closer to the data,55 5 We state Shortcut models in our time convention, in which t=0t=0 is data; the original formulation uses the reverse convention. 𝐱t−d′=𝐱t−d​sθ​(𝐱t,t,d),\mathbf{x}^{\prime}_{t-d}=\mathbf{x}_{t}-d\,s_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,d), so that r=t−dr=t-d in the notation of Section 2. As d→0d\to 0, the shortcut reduces to the instantaneous velocity.

Rather than regressing onto a teacher-defined target, Shortcut models exploit a self-consistency relation: one step of size 2​d2d should agree with two consecutive steps of size dd, sθ​(𝐱t,t,2​d)=12​sθ​(𝐱t,t,d)+12​sθ​(𝐱t−d′,t−d,d).s_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,2d)=\tfrac{1}{2}s_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,d)+\tfrac{1}{2}s_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}_{t-d},t-d,d). This yields a joint objective that combines flow matching at d=0d=0 with self-consistency at d>0d>0,

ℒS​(θ)=𝔼𝐱0∼pdata,ϵ∼𝒩⁡(𝟎,𝐈),(t,d)​[‖sθ​(𝐱t,t,0)−(ϵ−𝐱0)‖22+‖sθ​(𝐱t,t,2​d)−starget‖22],\mathcal{L}_{S}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_{0}\sim p_{\mathrm{data}},\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}),\,(t,d)}\left[\left\|s_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,0)-(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\mathbf{x}_{0})\right\|_{2}^{2}+\left\|s_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,2d)-s_{\mathrm{target}}\right\|_{2}^{2}\right], (10)

where starget=sg⁡(12​sθ​(𝐱t,t,d)+12​sθ​(𝐱t−d′,t−d,d))s_{\mathrm{target}}=\mathrm{sg}\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}s_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t},t,d)+\tfrac{1}{2}s_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime}_{t-d},t-d,d)\right) is constructed from the model’s own predictions. The flow-matching term anchors the model to the instantaneous velocity ϵ−𝐱0\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\mathbf{x}_{0}, while the self-consistency term propagates this capability from short steps to progressively larger ones, including the one-step setting.

Appendix E Extra Analyses on Flow Maps

E.1 Shortcut models

Setup.

Shortcut models (Frans et al., 2025) differ from MeanFlow in their task conditioning: instead of an endpoint time rr, the network receives the current noise level tt and a step size dd, so that 𝝉task=(t,d)\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{task}}=(t,d) and the endpoint is r=t−dr=t-d (Appendix D.3). We compute layerwise predictions (Eq. (2)) for a DiT-B/2 Shortcut model sθs_{\theta} trained on ImageNet (Russakovsky et al., 2015), using the two-step schedule 1→0.5→01\rightarrow 0.5\rightarrow 0, which corresponds to the two network evaluations sθ​(𝐳1,1,0.5)s_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{1},1,0.5) and sθ​(𝐳0.5,0.5,0.5)s_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{0.5},0.5,0.5) (Alg. E.1). From the shortcut predicted at block ii, sis_{i}, we decode the endpoint prediction with the model’s own update rule, 𝐱~t−di=𝐳t−d​si{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{t-d}^{\,i}}=\mathbf{z}_{t}-d\,s_{i}, and the diagnostic clean prediction 𝐱~0i=𝐳t−t​si{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{0}^{\,i}}=\mathbf{z}_{t}-t\,s_{i}. The first evaluation therefore decodes blockwise predictions of the noisy state 𝐳0.5\mathbf{z}_{0.5}, and the second decodes blockwise predictions of 𝐳0\mathbf{z}_{0}.

Observations. The Shortcut model shows the same denoise-then-renoise pattern as MeanFlow (Section 4.2). In the first step, whose endpoint 𝐱0.5\mathbf{x}_{0.5} is noisy, the layerwise predictions first reveal cleaner structure and then return toward the endpoint in the final blocks (Fig. 18, top), and ρ⁡(i)\rho(i) correspondingly decreases and then increases within the step (Fig. 18, bottom left). Depth as time thus extends to step-conditioned flow maps.

Frequency-domain signature. We also compute the radially averaged power spectrum of each endpoint prediction in the first step (Field, 1987, Simoncelli and Olshausen, 2001): for block ii, Pi​(ω)=|ℱ⁡[𝐱~t−di]​(ω)|2P_{i}(\omega)=|\mathcal{F}[{\color[rgb]{0.6914,0.1406,0.0938}\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_{t-d}^{\,i}}](\omega)|^{2}, averaged over frequencies of equal magnitude κ=‖ω‖2\kappa=\|\omega\|_{2} to give P¯i​(κ)\bar{P}_{i}(\kappa). Intermediate blocks shift power toward the clean-image spectrum, and later blocks shift it back toward the noisier endpoint spectrum (Fig. 18, bottom right), confirming the pattern in frequency space.
